  • Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust.

Industry observers note that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and fresh.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo states. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo claims. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive new display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot fresh multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Sources indicate that just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

It has been revealed that I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

According to recent reports, my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot newly introduced display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

According to recent reports, when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive newly introduced mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

Sources indicate that SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

According to recent reports, the new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

According to recent reports, the TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

Sources indicate that one sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

Industry observers note that you’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

In a recent development, the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

The TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

It has been revealed that hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Industry observers note that under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor problem. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Recent findings suggest that feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

According to recent reports, after skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

According to recent reports, the UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an patch for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

It has been revealed that TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a massive surprise.

When it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

According to recent reports, most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That stated, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

All of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of upcoming content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

As for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

In a recent development, all of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

Sources indicate that in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most crucial connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

Industry observers note that wiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Industry observers note that all the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s important to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

According to recent reports, each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is notable for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

If you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. The author of hundreds of articles, Ryan has a passion for finding readers the best value on the best gear out there.

  • Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

According to recent reports, as part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he mentioned.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Sources indicate that evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

Sources indicate that “Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign remarked in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”.

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Industry observers note that laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • In a recent development, intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, states Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

In a recent development, intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, states Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Recent findings suggest that well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

In a recent development, “Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys says. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

In a recent development, since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

In a recent development, and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea claims. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

Industry observers note that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holland America Line unveiled its 2028-29 Asia cruise season, marking the Eurodam’s debut in the region.

The season will run from September 2028 through May 2029, with itineraries ranging from 11 to 27 days.

Departing from Tokyo, Japan; Hong Kong, China; and Singapore, they will take guests to Japan, South Korea, China, Taiwan, the Philippines and Southeast Asia.

“Asia is one of those regions where you can experience something completely different from one port to the next, from a major city like Hong Kong to our newly introduced call at Coron in the Philippines, known for its turquoise waters and rich history,” stated Paul Grigsby, vice president of deployment and revenue planning for Holland America Line.

“That contrast is what makes these itineraries so interesting to build. The latest ports take guests beyond the places they may already know, introducing them to islands, coastlines and historic communities that reveal another side of the region, while natural phenomena like Japan’s cherry blossoms can make the experience completely different depending on when you visit.”.

Five fresh ports will be featured: Coron, Busuanga Island, Philippines, Hirara and Wakayama in Japan, Magong in Taiwan and Muara, a gateway to Brunei Darussalam.

Across the season, guests can enjoy overnight stays and late-night departures in 14 ports throughout the region, including two upcoming ones Keelung (Taipei) and Phú Mỹ (Ho Chi Minh City).

Recent findings suggest that as recently unveiled, there will also be a 27-day Coffee, Tea & Spice Route Legendary Voyage, departing Jan. 3 roundtrip from Singapore.

The Destination Dining program will bring the itinerary onboard, allowing guests to sample dishes including Japanese rockfish and fresh sushi, Korean bibimbap with beef bulgogi, Thai mango sticky rice, Filipino chicken adobo, and more.

For a limited time, when guests book 2028-2029 Asia cruises with the Have It All premium package, the standard package amenities of shore excursions, specialty dining, a Signature Beverage Package and Surf Wi-Fi are included.

There is also the added perk of free prepaid crew appreciation, along with free upgrades to the Elite Beverage Package and Premium Wi-Fi.

Guests can also take advantage of the Exclusive Mariner Society Early Booking Bonus and Mariner Society loyalty members can get up to $400 onboard credit per stateroom.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

Sources indicate that the GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

According to recent reports, white House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting fresh ways for this administration to defy Congress," remarked Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray remarked in a statement.

According to recent reports, sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters remarked.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

Industry observers note that "I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

Sources indicate that "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis remarked. "Both are bad.".

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

Recent findings suggest that and Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

In a recent development, he served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Industry observers note that before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

According to recent reports, ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

According to recent reports, former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

In a recent development, gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide at the moment serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

  • Industry observers note that like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube.
  • Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Industry observers note that like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

Industry observers note that roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, states his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”.

Damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, new models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

It has been revealed that while the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain fresh talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

Recent findings suggest that but a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, notes Paul Goodrum, PhD, a professor in Construction Engineering and Management at the University of Colorado Boulder. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he notes. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”.

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum claims: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”.

According to recent reports, the shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

According to recent reports, most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

Recent findings suggest that “For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” says Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”.

Recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the Fresh Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

Roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he claims, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”.

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

Industry News: AIDA Cruises Celebrates 30 Years of Partnership with Madeira

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (295 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cruiseindustrynews

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Madeira Ports Authority revealed that AIDA Cruises celebrated 30 years of partnership with the ports with a gathering on the AIDAprima on November 5 at the Port of Funchal, bringing together institutional partners and representatives of the cruise tourism sector.

The event, part of the cruise line’s “30 Years of Strong Partnership–Destination Dialogue: Shaping the Future Together” program, brought together the Madeira Ports Authority (APRAM, SA), Funchal City Council, AIDA’s shipping agents and shorex agents.

“AIDA Cruises is an notable partner for the Port of Funchal and Madeira, with a relationship spanning three decades that has contributed to the development and consolidation of cruise tourism in the Region,” said Paula Cabaco, chairwoman of the board of directors of the Madeira Ports Authority (APRAM, SA).

This relationship, she remarked, is built on trust, cooperation and joint efforts.

“For 30 years, AIDA and Madeira have shared a close and trusting partnership. We are sincerely grateful to our partners and the people of Madeira for the openness, hospitality and trust they have shown AIDA and our guests throughout these years,” mentioned Steffi Heinicke, senior vice president, guest experience and OBR, at AIDA Cruises. “We look forward to continuing this special partnership for many years to come.”.

According to the press release, AIDA Cruises’ ships made 40 calls to Madeira last year, representing more than 23 percent of the total number of passengers at the Port of Funchal.

APRAM added that the partnership has been developed by several entities, including Funchal City Council, and represented at the event by Vice-Mayor Carlos Rodrigues, tourism organizations, authorities and industry stakeholders.

The collaboration also has an environmental dimension, as seen with the tree-planting initiative at Funchal’s Ecological Park.

#65672. Tech Report: Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

Tech Report: Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed.
  • In a recent development, some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

In a recent development, some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

In a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

Industry observers note that at a similar manufacturer, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

It has been revealed that for some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

Cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

Sources indicate that this is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might plan to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

It works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

“Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

According to recent reports, the Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

At Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The organization also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment strategy. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

According to recent reports, there’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

And today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious concern in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fincantieri has unveiled more details about the two newly introduced ships it will build for Carnival Cruise Line.

Following yesterday’s announcement of a deal for the construction of latest vessels between the two companies, Fincantieri has now shared that the ships, scheduled for delivery in 2033 and 2035, will be built at its Marghera shipyard.

Fincantieri noted in a press release that the value of the contract is deemed “very crucial,” a designation it uses for agreements whose value exceeds €2 billion.

The ships will be 130,000 tons and have around 1,650 guest cabins each, the shipbuilder remarked.

The vessels will be dual-fuel powered, with LNG as their primary fuel.

Additionally, the upcoming design has been developed as a multi-brand platform for Carnival Corporation with a view to its potential future implementation across several of its cruise lines.

Industry observers note that “With 12 new ships now on order for delivery through 2039 across Carnival Cruise Line, Princess and AIDA, we have a strong pipeline that supports our measured approach to growth. The variety of ship sizes and features gives us flexibility to expand the choices and destinations we offer guests,” said Josh Weinstein, CEO of Carnival Corporation.

In a recent development, “At the same time, each fresh generation of ships brings advances in technology and efficiency that help us further reduce emissions and our overall environmental footprint. Fincantieri has been a terrific partner throughout this journey, and even after 76 ships and 30 years, there’s still something special about seeing the next one come to life.”.

In a recent development, pierroberto Folgiero, CEO and managing director of Fincantieri, noted: “Our relationship with Carnival Corporation continues to evolve through a shared ambition to push the boundaries of ship design, technological innovation and sustainability. These vessels embody a newly introduced paradigm of shipbuilding, where product innovation goes hand in hand with the transformation of our industrial system.”.

This follows the order for three upcoming Ace-class ships the duo revealed in July, the first of which, the Carnival Destiny, is already being built at the Monfalcone shipyard.

As previously reported, the first Ace-class vessel will carry the name previously used by the 1996-built Destiny.

Philipp Grasmug Joins MXP as CTO

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MarineXchange (MXP) has appointed Philipp Grasmug as its chief technology officer (CTO).

In this role, he will lead MXP’s technology strategy, product engineering and the continued development of the MXP Enterprise Platform, with a strong focus on security, scalability and AI.

Michael Eder, CEO of MXP, welcomed Grasmug to MXP, commenting: “As the leading software partner for the cruise industry, we attract top technology talent and leaders. Philipp’s experience in building and scaling business-critical software comes at exactly the right time as we take the next step in our growth story.”.

With more than 20 years of experience in developing complex software products for essential business operations, Grasmug most recently served as CTO of UBIMET Group, where he led 30 engineers and a global weather forecasting platform used by clients in insurance, critical infrastructure and renewable energy.

Fresh aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune mentioned of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an upgrade,” Tillis remarked. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy noted the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

In a recent development, “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy stated on CNBC Monday. “This can happen rapidly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he mentioned included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the fresh request specifically for air traffic control related challenges, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

Recent findings suggest that “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune stated. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the fresh funding request.

Sources indicate that “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., stated on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Brazilian court ordered the arrest of Corazul’s the Buenavista at the Port of Santos after the cruise line’s exclusive Brazilian distributor claimed it was owed about $270,000 (R$1.48 million), according to a court decision dated Nov. 13.

Judge Frederico dos Santos Messias of the São Paulo State Court of Justice’s specialized maritime court granted the request from R11 Travel Viagens e Turismo against GLCL Global Cruiseline Ltd., the Cyprus-registered company that operates as Corazul.

The judge issued the order without first hearing from Corazul, the decision showed.

Industry observers note that the order barred the Buenavista from leaving Brazilian waters. The court mentioned the ship was anchored off Santos for repairs.

The judge set security at about $323,000 (R$1.78 million) and said the ship would be released if Corazul deposited that amount or posted a bank guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that according to the decision, R11 noted Corazul owed about $1.27 million (R$6.96 million) under a four-year exclusive distribution agreement signed in March. That figure included about $780,000 (EUR 675,000) in unpaid quarterly marketing contributions. After subtracting about $1 million (R$5.48 million) in passenger funds it held, R11 put the net balance at about $270,000.

According to recent reports, the filing, as summarized by the court, described a series of disruptions including the cancellation of the Buenavista’s European season in June; the cancellation of its Oct. 23 inaugural Brazilian cruise nine days before departure and complaints about onboard service on the Oct. 30 sailing. The company has since suspended operations and R11 has stopped selling cruises on the ship.

It has been revealed that R11 noted Corazul demanded $400,000 on Nov. 4 before it would operate the Nov. 6 departure. R11 refused.

Sources indicate that the court noted that only two of the 11 sailings scheduled between Oct. 23 and Nov. 27 operated. Corazul also suspended operations until Nov. 30 and moved the end of its Brazil season up to March 5, 2027. The judge wrote that Corazul’s own communications demonstrated a “serious liquidity collapse.”.

The dispute is headed to arbitration in São Paulo under AMCHAM, the American Chamber of Commerce for Brazil. The decision stated that R11 must file within 30 days or the order lapses. Corazul has five days after being served to contest it.

#65666. Breaking: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (909 w)

Breaking: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • Sources indicate that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said.
  • In a recent development, in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, Upcoming Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

In a recent development, in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A significant takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Recent findings suggest that republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

It has been revealed that while there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

In a recent development, if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

According to recent reports, if one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 Wusongkou Forum took place on Nov. 8 at the Shanghai International Cruise Tourism Resort in Baoshan. It brought together regulators, port authorities, cruise operators and industry experts to discuss what organizers called “three-cruise synergy,” which is the coordinated development of ocean cruise ships, river cruise vessels and yachts.

According to recent reports, hosted by Shanghai Wusongkou Culture & Tourism Investment (Group) Co., the event included the launch of a “Three-Cruise Synergy · A New Voyage from River to Sea” program. Four initiatives were confirmed.

According to recent reports, the first is a “Cruise Plus” brand renewal blueprint. It targets four consumer segments: seniors, weddings and romance travel, sporting events and younger travelers. The goal is to turn passenger volume into more onboard and shoreside spending.

The second is a river-sea linkage project that uses Wusongkou’s location at the mouth of the Yangtze to connect inland river cities with ocean itineraries. Its flagship product is the Yangtze No. 3, which has begun sailing between Chongqing and Shanghai from the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal. It is the first river-sea cruise service to cover the full length of the Yangtze.

Industry observers note that third, China Huaxia International Cruise Co. released October 2026 data for its China Cruise Consumption Vitality Index. The manufacturer described it as the country’s first regular data tool for the cruise market.

The fourth initiative links the cruise terminal with Shanghai Baoshan railway station, which is due to open next year as the meeting point of the Shanghai–Chongqing–Chengdu high-speed line and the Shanghai–Nantong railway. Intends include combined rail and cruise ticketing, a direct shuttle, baggage transfer from car door to cabin door and shared VIP benefits.

On forum day, the Adora Magic City and the Adora Flora City, China’s first two domestically built large cruise ships, were berthed together at Wusongkou for the first time.

There’s Old San Juan, with all its pastel-painted façades, galleries and shops, blue cobblestone streets, and tucked-away restaurants; Condado and Ocean Park for long, sea-salty afternoons by the ocean; and Santurce, where street murals, galleries, haute dining, and a lively bar scene bring a fresh, creative vibe to the city.
