    #65552. Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1700 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency.
    • It has been revealed that the differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies.
    • An aircraft's wingtips play an important role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency. However, despite pursuing the same goal, all three aircraft feature noticeably different wingtip designs, ranging from distinctive split-tip winglets to swept-back extensions and even enormous folding wingtips.

    It has been revealed that the differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies. Instead, each design reflects a combination of aerodynamic performance, aircraft dimensions, and the practical limitations imposed by airports. Understanding why these aircraft have such different wingtips provides an interesting insight into the compromises involved in modern aircraft engineering.

    An aircraft's wingtips play an important role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise. As air moves around a wing, higher-pressure air beneath the wing attempts to move toward the lower-pressure region above it. This movement creates swirling vortices around the wingtips, which contribute to a phenomenon known as induced drag. The resulting resistance makes it harder for an aircraft to maintain speed and requires additional engine thrust.

    Recent findings suggest that reducing induced drag is therefore a major consideration when manufacturers design new commercial aircraft. One of the most straightforward ways to achieve this is by increasing the wingspan, effectively distributing lift across a longer wing and reducing the strength of the vortices produced at its extremities. However, making wings longer introduces another challenge, since airports have strict limits on how much space aircraft can occupy.

    In a recent development, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) establishes aircraft size categories that help airports determine which aircraft can use particular gates, taxiways, and other infrastructure. These categories are largely determined by wingspan, meaning manufacturers cannot simply make every aircraft's wings as long as they would ideally like. An aircraft that exceeds the relevant dimensions could require different airport facilities, potentially limiting its operational flexibility.

    Boeing's engineers must consequently balance aerodynamic efficiency against the practical requirements of commercial aviation. Different wingtip devices offer different ways to manage this compromise. Some extend the effective wing vertically, while others increase the actual wingspan or combine both approaches. The three aircraft demonstrate how these engineering decisions can produce substantially different solutions to essentially the same aerodynamic problem.

    In a recent development, the Boeing 737 MAX features perhaps the most visually distinctive wingtip arrangement of the three aircraft. Its Advanced Technology winglets have two separate extensions, with one pointing upward and another extending downward. This split-tip configuration gives the aircraft a distinctive appearance while helping reduce induced drag without requiring a substantial increase in its overall wingspan.

    It has been revealed that the reason Boeing selected this particular arrangement becomes clearer when considering the aircraft's relationship with the 737 Next Generation family. The Boeing 737 MAX was developed to retain considerable operational commonality with its predecessors, allowing airlines to introduce the newer aircraft without requiring significant changes to their existing airport infrastructure. Keeping its wingspan within the ICAO Code C limit of 118 feet (36 meters) was therefore an important design consideration.

    According to recent reports, A conventional raked wingtip, such as the arrangement found on the Boeing 787, would have extended the 737 MAX's wings too far horizontally. This could have pushed the aircraft outside the dimensions associated with its existing airport category, creating complications for airlines operating it alongside older 737 variants. The split-tip design improved aerodynamic performance while keeping the aircraft within its required dimensional limits.

    According to recent reports, the winglets also incorporate carefully shaped surfaces designed to manage airflow and reduce aerodynamic losses. Rather than simply adding extensions to the existing wing, Boeing developed a more sophisticated arrangement intended to improve overall efficiency. This was particularly key for an aircraft that needed to deliver better fuel economy while retaining much of the operational flexibility that had made earlier 737 generations attractive to airlines.

    The latest data from ch-aviation demonstrates that Southwest Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737 MAX, with a total of 300 in its fleet, followed by United Airlines with 243.

    According to recent reports, unlike the 737 MAX, the Boeing 787 was developed as an entirely latest aircraft family, giving Boeing considerably more freedom when designing its wings. Rather than adopting conventional vertical winglets, the manufacturer opted for long, swept-back raked wingtips that extend the wing horizontally. The result is a particularly elegant design that contributes to the 787's distinctive appearance.

    It has been revealed that the Boeing 787's wing design was developed with aerodynamic efficiency as a central priority, rather than being constrained by the dimensional requirements associated with an existing narrowbody aircraft family. Its larger wingspan allows the aircraft to benefit from the reduced induced drag associated with longer wings. Boeing was therefore able to pursue a solution that offered aerodynamic advantages without introducing conventional upward-pointing winglets.

    Research from Boeing and NASA indicates that raked wingtips can reduce drag by approximately 5.5%, compared with improvements of around 3.5% to 4.5% for conventional winglets. Although the precise benefits depend on the aircraft and operating conditions, these figures help explain why Boeing selected this configuration for its widebody aircraft. The design also avoids some of the additional structural weight associated with separate winglet structures.

    United Airlines is right now the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787, as outlined in the table below:.

    Recent findings suggest that another notable characteristic of the Boeing 787's wings is their composite construction. Built primarily from advanced carbon-fiber-reinforced materials, they are designed to be long, relatively thin, and flexible. This flexibility allows the wings to respond to aerodynamic forces during flight, while their overall shape contributes to improved efficiency. Combined with the raked wingtips, the design helps the 787 achieve the aerodynamic performance required for long-distance commercial operations.

    The Boeing 777X takes the concept of longer wings considerably further, featuring the largest wingspan of any commercial airliner currently designed for airline service. Its wings extend 235 feet (72 meters) when fully deployed. This substantial span helps reduce induced drag and supports the aircraft's objective of delivering improved fuel efficiency on long-haul routes.

    However, the Boeing 777X faces a practical problem that the 787 does not encounter to the same extent. Its enormous wingspan would exceed the dimensions permitted within the ICAO Code E category used by many large commercial aircraft. This could make it difficult for the aircraft to operate at airports designed around the existing infrastructure used by conventional widebody aircraft, potentially restricting where airlines could deploy it.

    Boeing's solution was to develop folding wingtips that allow the outer sections of the wings to rotate upward while the aircraft is on the ground. Once folded, the 777X's wingspan is reduced to just under 213 feet (65 m), bringing it within the dimensional requirements associated with Code E airport operations. Before take-off, the wingtips extend into their normal flight positions, restoring the aircraft's full aerodynamic configuration.

    This arrangement is particularly interesting because it allows Boeing to avoid choosing between aerodynamic performance and airport compatibility. The aircraft can benefit from an exceptionally long wing during flight without requiring airports to accommodate its entire wingspan while parked or taxiing. The folding mechanism adds engineering complexity, but it provides a practical solution to a problem that would otherwise have required substantial compromises in wing design.

    The Boeing 777X is set to become the latest and largest member of the manufacturer's successful 777 family. Designed to offer improved efficiency, greater range, and increased passenger comfort, the aircraft will be available in three variants: the 777-8 and 777-9 passenger models, along with the 777-8F cargo aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will be the first variant to enter service, offering airlines a high-capacity long-haul aircraft. The smaller 777-8 will provide greater range, while the freighter version targets the growing cargo market.

    However, the program has experienced considerable delays. Originally expected to enter service in 2020, the Boeing 777X has faced certification challenges, flight-testing setbacks, and problems involving its fresh GE9X engines. As of November 2026, Boeing is targeting the first 777-9 delivery in 2027. The 777-8F is expected around two years later, while the passenger 777-8 is not anticipated before 2030. Despite the setbacks, the 777X remains an notable part of Boeing's future long-haul aircraft aims.

    In a recent development, emirates is set to be the world's largest operator of the Boeing 777X, with a staggering 270 on order. The carriers with the largest firm orders for the passenger variants of the 777X (777-8 and 777-9) are outlined in the table below:.

    Although the three Boeing aircraft use different solutions, their wingtip designs are based on the same aerodynamic principles. All three aim to reduce induced drag, improve lift distribution, and lower the amount of energy required to maintain efficient flight. The differences emerge because each aircraft operates within a different set of dimensional and engineering constraints, rather than because Boeing has changed its overall approach to aerodynamic efficiency.

    Industry observers note that for the Boeing 737 MAX, airport compatibility was particularly important because the aircraft needed to retain the operational flexibility of the previous 737 generation. Its split-tip winglets provide aerodynamic improvements without substantially increasing its wingspan, making them a practical solution for a narrowbody aircraft operating across a wide variety of airports.

    In a recent development, the Boeing 787 had greater design freedom, allowing Boeing to prioritize aerodynamic performance through a longer wing and swept-back raked wingtips. Its composite construction also makes it possible to develop a lightweight, flexible wing structure that works particularly well with this configuration. The absence of conventional winglets is therefore a deliberate engineering decision, not an omission.

    Meanwhile, the Boeing 777X represents a different approach altogether, combining the aerodynamic advantages of an exceptionally long wing with a folding mechanism that addresses airport limitations. Its design demonstrates how manufacturers can use mechanical innovation to overcome restrictions that would otherwise prevent them from pursuing more ambitious aerodynamic improvements.

    Together, these three aircraft show that there is no single ideal wingtip design for every commercial aircraft, since the most effective solution ultimately depends on the aircraft's size, intended operations, and the infrastructure it must use.

    Restored to Calder’s initiative, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • Industry observers note that fifty years later, Alexander S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    Industry observers note that fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    According to recent reports, “It’s totally phenomenal,” he noted, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    According to recent reports, it was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Recent findings suggest that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he remarked. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he stated. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and stated he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he stated. “Nobody got how substantial this was until it highlighted up on their doorstep.”.

    Quilici mentioned he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    In a recent development, “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    In a recent development, “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

    According to recent reports, in addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

    Sources indicate that according to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he remarked, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he noted.

    Recent findings suggest that younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he stated, gazing up at it.

    According to recent reports, ‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

    Sources indicate that I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

    Recent findings suggest that brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

    After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

    The carrier noted Friday that it will restart flights from Fresh York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

    According to recent reports, american has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

    According to recent reports, israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and Newly introduced York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

    Sources indicate that american also remarked Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

    The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

    Sources indicate that “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between Fresh York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

    Industry observers note that israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Latest York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the concern is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    Recent findings suggest that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    Sources indicate that at problem is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    According to recent reports, the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Fresh York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Industry observers note that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly remarked it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the glitch.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

    Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump stated, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Industry observers note that trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    Sources indicate that “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most vital stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations mentioned. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

    It has been revealed that “Across the political spectrum,” the letter noted, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to upcoming national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    The Mid-Size Florida Hub Betting $1.5 Billion That Delta Air Lines Will Turn It Into An International Gateway

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age.
    • Tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037.
    • It has been revealed that delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    Tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037. Structural steel will begin going up this Summer, with completion targeted for late 2028 and a public opening in 2029. It is the airport's first new airside terminal in nearly 20 years.

    It has been revealed that delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge. The commitment is the longest and most substantial terminal agreement Delta has made at any mid-size Florida airport. It positions Tampa as a potential international gateway for the airline once the new Federal Inspection Services facility gives the airport the processing capacity to support widebody international arrivals.

    In a recent development, TPA is building its first fresh airside terminal in nearly 20 years. The Hillsborough County Aviation Authority Board approved the 100% final design for Airside D on February 5, clearing the project for full construction. The facility will be 600,000 square feet (55,742 sq meters) with 16 gates serving both domestic and international flights.

    It has been revealed that it includes a new Federal Inspection Services area for processing international arrivals, an 8-lane security checkpoint, and a new checked baggage inspection system in the main terminal. The total project cost is $1.528 billion, including a $902 million supplemental contract approved in late 2025.

    Construction is well underway. A 300-ton crane is erecting the structural steel framework, which consists of 6,200 tons of steel comprising over 7,300 individual pieces connected by 96,000 bolts and 212,000 inches of welding. Approximately 200 workers are on site daily, with that number expected to increase significantly as the project moves from structural work into mechanical, electrical, and interior fit-out phases.

    HNTB designed the project, the same firm that designed TPA's existing main terminal and automated people mover system. Completion is targeted for late 2028 with a public opening in 2029. Once operational, Airside D will increase TPA's total gate count and expand the airport's annual passenger capacity from its current 25 million to 35 million by 2037.

    Industry observers note that the airport handled approximately 24 million passengers in 2024, meaning it is approaching the capacity limits of its existing terminal complex. Airside D provides the infrastructure to accommodate the growth TPA has been experiencing without the crowding and gate constraints that would otherwise limit airline expansion at the airport.

    Delta was selected as the anchor tenant for Airside D in a decision unveiled by the Hillsborough County Aviation Authority. The lease covers at least six of the 16 gates on a 20-year term, giving Delta a dedicated presence in the new facility through approximately 2049. The agreement includes a mezzanine-level Delta Sky Club, the carrier's first purpose-built lounge at TPA.

    It has been revealed that the remaining 10 gates will be available for other carriers, with the airport authority retaining flexibility to assign them based on demand and airline interest. A 20-year anchor lease at a mid-size airport is not a routine commitment. Delta operates from dozens of airports across the United States, but it signs long-term anchor agreements only at facilities where it intends to build or sustain a significant operation over multiple decades.

    Recent findings suggest that the lease term matches the terminal's useful life, meaning Delta is committing to Tampa for as long as Airside D operates. The Sky Club inclusion signals that Delta expects enough premium traffic at TPA to justify the capital investment and ongoing operating cost of a dedicated lounge, which the airline typically reserves for its largest hubs and busiest focus cities.

    Sources indicate that delta right now operates approximately 45 daily departures from Tampa to destinations including Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Salt Lake City, New York-JFK, Boston, and Amsterdam. The Amsterdam route, operated on the A330-900, is Delta's first year-round widebody international service from TPA.

    It serves as a proof of concept for the kind of European flying the airline could expand from Airside D once the facility opens. The six-gate commitment in a terminal with a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area positions Delta to add additional international routes from Tampa without competing for gate space or customs processing capacity in the airport's existing international facility.

    Delta operates the largest domestic hub-and-spoke network of any US carrier. It is built around hubs at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Sources indicate that atlanta is the largest by a wide margin, handling over 1,000 daily Delta departures and serving as the airline's primary connecting hub for domestic and international traffic. Delta's existing Florida footprint is substantial but spread across multiple airports without a dominant hub presence at any single one.

    It has been revealed that the airline operates from Orlando International Airport (MCO), Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Miami International Airport (MIA), Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), and TPA, among others. None of those airports functions as a Delta hub in the way that Atlanta or Detroit do.

    However, Orlando and Fort Lauderdale carry the highest Florida frequencies, driven by leisure demand from Delta's Northeastern and Midwestern hubs. The anchor tenant commitment does not make Tampa a hub. Delta is not building a connecting operation at TPA comparable to what it runs at Atlanta or Detroit.

    The lease establishes Tampa as a long-term focus city with dedicated infrastructure, a premium lounge, and the physical capacity to grow well beyond the 45 daily departures Delta at the moment operates. The distinction matters because a focus city with a 20-year lease and a purpose-built Sky Club receives a different level of investment and scheduling priority than a station where the airline operates from shared gates on short-term agreements.

    Sources indicate that TPA already handles international flights. Edelweiss serves Zurich, Avianca recently introduced daily service to Bogota, and Delta added year-round Amsterdam service. Caribbean and Canadian routes to destinations including San Juan, Toronto, Montreal, Cancun, and Santo Domingo operate from the existing terminal.

    It has been revealed that the airport is not starting international service from zero. What it lacks is the capacity to grow it meaningfully beyond what the current Federal Inspection Services facility can process. Airside D's dedicated FIS area changes that constraint. The upcoming facility will have its own Customs and Border Protection processing area capable of handling widebody international arrivals simultaneously with domestic operations on the same concourse.

    Industry observers note that delta's six gates in a terminal with FIS capability give the airline the infrastructure to operate international flights from Tampa without competing for processing capacity in the airport's existing international arrivals facility. Routes to London, Paris, or additional European destinations that require a full international arrivals hall become operationally feasible in a way they are not today from Delta's current gate positions.

    According to recent reports, the most striking figure in the airport authority's route development materials is the leakage rate. Approximately 50% of Tampa's international origin-and-destination traffic currently uses other Florida airports, primarily MIA, MCO, and FLL.

    Tampa Bay area residents flying internationally drive to other airports because nonstop international options from TPA are limited. Airside D's FIS capacity, combined with Delta's anchor presence and the gate infrastructure to support widebody international service, is designed to recapture that leakage by giving Tampa the facilities to offer the international routes its local market already demands.

    The Tampa Bay metropolitan area is one of the fastest-growing regions in the US. The four-county metro area comprising Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, and Hernando counties has added over 400,000 residents since 2010 and now exceeds 3.3 million people. The region's economy has diversified beyond its traditional tourism and military base.

    Indeed, the finance, healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors are driving corporate travel demand alongside the leisure traffic that has historically defined Florida aviation. TPA handled 24.5 million passengers in fiscal year 2025, approaching the 25 million capacity ceiling the airport authority identified as the trigger point for Airside D.

    Sources indicate that the 2029 opening timing aligns with several fleet developments at Delta. Namely, Delta's Airbus A350-1000 deliveries will begin in late 2026, freeing up A330-900s and A350-900s that could be deployed on international routes from secondary hubs and focus cities, including Tampa.

    Delta's year-round Amsterdam service, introduced on the A330-900, is a proof of concept for European widebody service from TPA. If the route performs well through 2027 and 2028, additional European destinations from Airside D's gates become a natural extension of the strategy once the facility opens.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    It has been revealed that seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom declared Friday.

    Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    Industry observers note that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    In a recent development, american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A fresh reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

    Sources indicate that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

    Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

    The airline unveiled its latest corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

    In a recent development, the most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

    The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

    In a recent development, iberia’s upcoming branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

    Sources indicate that the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

    The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The newly introduced appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

    It has been revealed that iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

    According to recent reports, the current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

    Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

    • It has been revealed that although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition. Locked in the endlessly escalating arms race with the Soviet Union, the US Air Force has commissioned an engineering study into a flying, nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. On September 12, 1969, Lockheed engineers G. Daniel Brewer, S. Dalton, and P. J. Sibley filed a manufacturer report LR-22802, outlining a machine that seemed to defy physics.

    It was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil. The mothership was expected to haul at least 22 McDonnell Douglas fighter jets on massive underwing pylons in the same way that the smaller planes carried missiles. Designated the CL-1201, the behemoth 'lightning' carrier would be capable of reaching any conflict zone in hours and promised to cruise for 41 straight days without resupply.

    It has been revealed that although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress. Popular accounts of the program claim that the USAF did in fact commission an active service example. However, no records to date, including the most detailed public file NASA, recorded as Memorandum X-2386, show that any order was officially lodged.

    The CL-1201's propulsion abandoned standard jet fuel logistics in favor of an unproven liquid-metal-cooled reactor delivering 1,830 megawatts of thermal energy. That staggering heat drove four mammoth aft turbofans at Mach 0.8 at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), offering effectively unlimited global range. The design aimed to bypass the need for any overseas airfields and reliance on allied partners entirely by maintaining an airborne presence for over a month, limited only by crew endurance and engine oil.

    The primary CL-1201-1-1 Attack Aircraft Carrier variant would house a crew of 845 to operate 22 fighters beneath its wings. Meanwhile, the alternative CL-1201-1-3 Logistics Support Aircraft traded strike fighters for a cavernous cargo bay. It was proposed with the capacity to deploy an entire combat brigade of 3,896 soldiers with 6,207 tons (5,631 metric tons) of equipment to any hot spot on the globe.

    In a recent development, eight years before Lockheed's engineers filed their report, US President John F. Kennedy had already canceled the US aircraft nuclear propulsion program. After 15 years of research, it was finally called off in 1961. The numbers had never successfully solved all the safety complications with installing an active nuclear reactor in an airplane. Two airships, the USS Akron and Macon, preceded the C-1201 as early motherships, and one Convair NB-36H had been equipped with nuclear power plants for test flights.

    Yet, scientists were unable to ever create an atomic engine considered safe enough to not have a devastating environmental impact in the event of a mishap. Furthermore, turning the CL-1201 concept into an airworthy airframe demanded solving the immediate physics problem of how to lift nearly 12 million lb (5.4 million kg) into the sky. No airport on Earth could handle the landing gear footprint, forcing the design team to adopt a complex propulsion compromise.

    It has been revealed that the retrieval system of the CL-1201 lowered a hydraulically stabilized pantograph hook 35 feet (10.7 meters) beneath the airframe into clean, undisturbed air. A docking fighter pilot engaged the hook with a dorsal latch, allowing heavy winches to haul the aircraft up against cradle stops before swinging it into internal maintenance bays. This acrobatic aerial recovery demanded precision flying in high-altitude crosswinds, turning routine combat patrols into dangerous flight-test maneuvers that risked pilot lives.

    Sources indicate that docking a 40,000-lb (18,140 kg) fighter beneath a 125,000-square-foot (11,613 sq m) wing generated lethal aerodynamic turbulence that tested the limits of human piloting. Incoming flight crews had to fly through a violent boundary layer wake and wingtip vortex wash, with velocity spikes exceeding 120 feet (37 meters) per second. The chaotic upwash threatened to smash approaching jets against the lower wing skin, prompting designers to engineer an articulated trapeze boom.

    Beyond the docking challenges, Cold War missile advances made the carrier extraordinarily vulnerable to long-range Soviet surface-to-air missile networks. The tailless 560-foot (171-meter) airframe would look like staring into the sun on an enemy's radar scope. Its gigantic profile would create an immense radar target that air defense systems like the Soviet S-200 Angara could spot hundreds of miles away. A single missile strike could instantly wipe out an entire combat wing and crack open the central atomic reactor.

    At a gross weight of 11.85 million lb (5.4 million kg), roughly fifteen times the mass of a Boeing 747 or Lockheed C-5 Galaxy, the CL-1201 exceeded the limits of every runway in the world. Standard concrete aprons would be crushed under its landing gear, while constructing dedicated five-mile runways around the world negated the strategic autonomy that justified it. To eliminate runway dependence, engineering lead Brewer and his team adopted an extreme vertical takeoff and landing design.

    It has been revealed that rather than routing reactor thermal energy to lift fans, the configuration housed 182 dedicated jet-fuel-powered turbojets in retractable forward fuselage bays and inner wing banks. It would dramatically scale up the multi-engine vertical lift concept of experimental aircraft at the time, like the Dornier Do 31 and Yakovlev Yak 38. Each turbine was rated for 90,000 pounds of thrust for a combined vertical output of 16.38 million pounds.

    According to recent reports, in operational practice, this propulsion created severe liabilities at every launch site. Simultaneous ignition of 182 lift jets projected a 1,400°F downward exhaust plume capable of spalling reinforced concrete, liquefying asphalt, and generating severe foreign object damage hazards across massive areas. Furthermore, the lift engines would consume nearly 1.9 million lb (0.8 million kg) of JP-5 fuel during a single five-minute departure sequence, burning the equivalent fuel capacity of six fully loaded C-5 Galaxies before the nuclear engines engaged.

    Industry observers note that additionally, synchronizing 182 independent turbines during the low-speed transition from jet-borne hover to wing-borne aerodynamic flight introduced an alarmingly long list of potential failure points. A compressor stall or flameout within an outboard wing bank would generate violent asymmetric roll moments far exceeding the control authority of aerodynamic flight surfaces at near-zero airspeed. Ultimately, the CL 1201 was simply unviable due to its inability to break away from conventional infrastructure and limitations because of its size and not its power source, relegating the concept to a Cold War 'flight of fancy.'.

    In the 1940s and 1950s, the USAF and Atomic Energy Commission spent roughly $1 billion over 15 years on the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, hoping to build bombers that could stay airborne for weeks. The Convair NB-36H Crusader flew 47 test missions over Texas and Upcoming Mexico carrying an operational, air-cooled 1-to-3 megawatt reactor in its aft bomb bay. The bomber's entire nose had a 12-ton lead and rubber shield, complete with 12-inch-thick lead-glass windows.

    It has been revealed that adding the 17.5-ton reactor meant the aircraft had to haul nearly 30 tons of nuclear hardware and shielding before carrying any weapons. Every test flight was shadowed by a C-97 transport plane carrying a platoon of US Marines trained to parachute into the crash site and cordon off radioactive debris. Engineers could not solve the dilemma of making a reactor light enough without sacrificing containment. Furthermore, advances in intercontinental ballistic missiles and aerial refueling made nuclear bombers strategically obsolete.

    It has been revealed that lockheed aimed to overcome those limitations with an atomic propulsion plant rated at an astonishing 5,470 megawatts in a dual-circuit closed loop. Liquid lithium circulated through the primary reactor core at temperatures reaching 2,000°F (1,093°C), carrying thermal energy into an intermediate heat exchanger mounted inside a central structural containment cell. The secondary circuit circulated non-radioactive liquid alloy through pipes to four massive trailing-edge turbofans.

    The engines used single-stage titanium fan disks spanning an unprecedented 28 feet (8.5 meters) across. The liquid metal radiators sat directly behind the 14-stage axial compressors, transferring heat into the compressed air stream to produce 300,000 pounds of thrust (1,334 kN) per engine. Containing the energy required a titanium keel and trusses that were eight inches (20 cm) thick, as well as a shield of lead, tungsten, and borated water weighing 1.2 million lb (544,300 kg).

    Commissioned in the early 1930s, the USS Akron (ZRS-4) and her sister ship USS Macon (ZRS-5) were 785-foot-long rigid helium airships. Each airship housed an internal hangar bay holding up to five Curtiss F9C-2 Sparrowhawk biplanes. To launch, a mechanical 'trapeze' lowered a fighter beneath the airship's hull into the slipstream, where the pilot released a skyhook and flew away. To recover, the pilot matched the airship's 70-knot speed and snagged the trapeze bar with a hook mounted above the upper wing.

    On April 4, 1933, the Akron was caught in a violent thunderstorm off the coast of New Jersey. Downdrafts forced the tail into the Atlantic Ocean, breaking the airship apart. Less than two years later, on February 12, 1935, the Macon encountered a storm off Point Sur, California. Wind shear tore away her upper tail fin, puncturing rear gas cells and causing her to lose buoyancy and settle into the Pacific.

    Before the tragic and catastrophic demise of each airship, the trapeze system actually worked well, and the Navy never lost a plane during an in-flight catch. Despite successful fighter operations, the loss of the Macon ended the US Navy's permanent pursuit of flying aircraft carriers, and there's no indication that they ever revealed interest in the massive Lockheed concept. Meanwhile, the CL-1201 aimed to take this ill-fated earlier attempt and supersize it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., remarked he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday demonstrated how poisonous the politics could become.
    • According to recent reports, budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., remarked he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday demonstrated how poisonous the politics could become.

    According to recent reports, budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking crucial.”.

    Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    In a recent development, "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he stated on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson remarked Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    In a recent development, johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he mentioned.

    Industry observers note that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    Sources indicate that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a strategy in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability concern, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online.
    • Sources indicate that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants.
    • Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    Sources indicate that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    In a recent development, citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    According to recent reports, but Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    It has been revealed that like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    It has been revealed that generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    It has been revealed that unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    In a recent development, if you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    Recent findings suggest that but with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi states statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    Recent findings suggest that in many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    According to recent reports, if a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

    #65538. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1598 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    But the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the New Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    Passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or New Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    According to recent reports, moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    Legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    In a recent development, we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    Our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    Sources indicate that few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    Sources indicate that we would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    Sources indicate that the 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    If a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    #65537. Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1500 w)
