    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US.
    • According to recent reports, united right now operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B.
    • In 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US. All of American Airlines' ten hub airports are located within the continental US, as are all of Delta's nine hub airports. United Airlines, however, has seven hub airports in the continental US, as well as a hub in Guam, an overseas territory of the US located thousands of miles away from Washington. It's the only such operation by any US airline, and it carries on the legacy of an operation that goes back nearly 60 years.

    According to recent reports, united right now operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM). It is the start/end for the carrier's famous 'Island Hopper' service, and the airline also runs direct services from GUM to San Francisco with a stopover in Honolulu. This route uses a Boeing 777-300ER, while the rest of the GUM routes use the Boeing 737. United is by far the largest airline serving Guam, and it also serves as a vital link connecting Guam to the outside world.

    In 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands. Operating under the callsign 'Air Mike', the airline initially operated Boeing 727s and became a crucial component in the region's economic development during the late 20th century. Air Micronesia held a near monopoly in the market, and its 727s were crucial in connecting what were previously remote islands to the outside world.

    Continental would eventually own 100% of Air Micronesia, rebranding the airline to 'Continental Micronesia' while the headquarters eventually shifted to Guam. While other airlines attempted to connect Guam to the US at certain points and others served Micronesia from foreign countries, Continental Micronesia was by far the largest airline in this market. Among its most famous routes was the 'Island Hopper', connecting Guam to Honolulu with five stopovers, and the airline also had a substantial international network.

    In 1999, Continental Micronesia began transitioning from using the 727 to the 737NG for most operations, and in 2003, the Guam International Airport Facility pushed commuter airlines out of GUM's Commuter Terminal and leased the facility to Continental. The airline would become Guam's largest private-sector employer, while connecting GUM to over 20 destinations.

    Industry observers note that in 2010, Continental Airlines declared that it would merge with United Airlines, keeping the United name. In 2017, Continental Micronesia was formally merged into United Airlines (it had previously operated as a subsidiary of United Continental Holdings), and today, all Guam flights are directly operated by United.

    Airlines are hardly afraid of shutting down unprofitable hubs, and United itself dehubbed the Cleveland hub that it also inherited from Continental during the merger in 2014. However, the Guam operations were making money for the airline, and they're a vital link to the communities served. In addition, United absolutely dominates Guam, and the hub offers a unique strategic position within the carrier's network that couldn't otherwise be replicated by another hub.

    Guam itself is a hub for lucrative military and government activity, and United's position in Guam means that it essentially receives all government travel contracts. Because of the airline's dominance in GUM, it can also charge high fares due to the lack of competition. Altogether, Guam is actually one of United's most lucrative hubs, even if it is also one of its smallest. The operation makes the airline money, and so it will remain a United hub, even as other US legacy carriers have dehubbed their hubs outside of the US mainland.

    Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Denver International Airport (DEN).

    Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

    Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM).

    San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

    Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

    Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

    In March 2026, the carrier began transitioning from using the 737-800 to the 737 MAX 8 for its Guam operations, with the switch having been completed in October. These ten aircraft feature a significantly upgraded interior compared to the old 737-800s, and they feature signs in English and Japanese rather than English and Spanish, while the front row of economy can be collapsed to accommodate a stretcher for medevac flights. In addition, two United First seats are blocked on the Island Hopper to be used as a pilot crew rest facility.

    Going into the 2010s, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines both operated hubs at Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT). These hubs had operated for decades (Delta inherited NRT operations from Northwest Airlines, while United acquired the NRT routes from Pan Am) and essentially connected US passengers to Asia, serving as a central hub. But in the mid-2010s, United gradually discontinued intra-Asia routes out of NRT, and Delta exited NRT entirely in 2020 (it will return in 2027 with a single route from Seattle).

    Whereas United's Guam hub primarily serves the local market, the NRT hubs operated by United and Delta mainly existed for connections. However, the arrival of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 allowed these airlines to serve more destinations in Asia nonstop from the US, and nonstop flights typically earn a fare premium over one-stop options. As such, the NRT hubs weren't necessary anymore, since they were essentially set up due to range limitations of older widebodies like the Boeing 747-200.

    In addition to the improved economics of latest widebody aircraft, United announced a joint venture with All Nippon Airways in 2011, while Delta announced a joint venture with Korean Air in 2017. With these, the intra-Asia routes are covered by their joint venture partners, eliminating the need to operate these flights with their own metal. In other words, United's NRT hub has been replaced by nonstop flights to Asia and ANA's operations out of Tokyo, while Delta's NRT hub has been replaced by Korean Air's hub in Seoul.

    In a recent development, apart from the carrier's one-stop flight from GUM to San Francisco via Honolulu with the 777-300ER, all of United's Guam routes now use the 737 MAX 8. There are right now ten of them stationed in GUM, and they operate to Taipei, Manila, Airai, Saipan, Yap, Pohnpei, Chuuk, Tokyo Narita, Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, and Nagoya. In addition, the airline's flight to Airai continues to Manila on some days of the week, while the flight to Chuuk is part of the Island Hopper, flying from Guam to Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, and Majuro.

    Recent findings suggest that several of these routes do not operate daily, as local demand is ultimately limited and the 737 MAX 8 is a relatively large aircraft, able to carry up to 166 passengers in United's configuration. Japan is United's largest market out of GUM, as it connects the airport to four airports in Japan while operating up to five daily flights between GUM and Japan. Notably, United does not serve Nagoya from the mainland US nonstop.

    Some of these routes can be extremely long, which makes the fuel savings of the 737 MAX 8 over the 737-800 highly impactful. Meanwhile, the 777-300ER is flown to Guam almost entirely due to strong demand for cargo, as this is the aircraft in United's fleet with the highest cargo capacity. The airline only has 22 of these planes, which make up less than 10% of its overall widebody fleet, and yet the cargo revenue is strong enough to justify its use on the San Francisco-Honolulu-Guam route.

    While United's Guam operations have generally been successful, the hub has been facing difficulties in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as a decline in demand from Japan, the largest market for the hub. Ordinarily, United may simply shift capacity to another hub, but that isn't easy to do with Guam. The airport is thousands of miles away from any of United's other hubs, the carrier has a pilot and flight attendant base in Guam, and the ten 737s are specially configured for these services.

    What United has done with these assets is move them back to NRT. In recent years, the carrier has rolled out upcoming fifth freedom routes from NRT to Cebu, Kaohsiung, and Ulaanbaatar, using the flight numbers of the carrier's nonstop flights to NRT from the mainland US and operating the flights with Guam-based 737s. Crucially, these destinations are not served by ANA, which means that United is expanding the joint venture's Asia coverage while deploying assets that would have otherwise been underutilized.

    In a recent development, it's one of the most creative ways to utilize assets when the standard operation is no longer producing the returns that it once did. Not only that, but the airline has generated tremendous excitement and publicity over these routes, with the Ulaanbaatar route standing out in particular, and this is beneficial for loyalty program and credit card sign-ups, which is where the carrier makes its real money.

    • A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • It has been revealed that the county unveiled this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • According to recent reports, according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    It has been revealed that the county unveiled this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    According to recent reports, according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The upcoming lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

    The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

    TAP Air Portugal will launch a newly introduced thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

    TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the newly introduced IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

    It has been revealed that the newly introduced Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United prepares to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

    International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium highlights.

    IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the upcoming Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

    This content is hosted by Instagram.

    And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

    TAP’s latest OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

    The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate aims to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

    Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

    Industry observers note that US airlines regularly deploy widebody aircraft on domestic routes, especially between major hubs and airports with significant connecting traffic. According to scheduling data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, thousands of domestic widebody flights are scheduled between December and October next year. Delta Air Lines alone has scheduled more than 17,000 domestic widebody flights, including around 660 operated by the Airbus A350-900.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the shortest routes on which the airline had planned to deploy the aircraft was the roughly one-hour flight between Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). However, in its latest weekend schedule update, the SkyTeam member removed the A350 from that sector.

    It has been revealed that delta had scheduled the A350-900 on the Las Vegas-to-Los Angeles route on just three occasions in January 2027. It was originally assigned to flight DL39 on January 4 and 5, departing Las Vegas at 19:05 and arriving in Los Angeles at 20:22. A third service, operating as DL8783, was scheduled for January 3 with the same departure and arrival times.

    It has been revealed that according to AeroLOPA, the Atlanta-based carrier has two configurations of its A350-900 aircraft. The first accommodates 306 passengers, with 32 business class seats, 48 premium economy seats and 226 economy seats. The second has 275 seats, comprising 40 in business class, 40 in premium economy and 195 in economy. Delta had planned to deploy the latter configuration.

    It has been revealed that the planned A350-900 deployment may have been linked to the Consumer Electronics Show (CES), an annual technology trade show taking place in Las Vegas from January 6 to 9. The event attracts visitors from around the world, and Delta is increasing its services to the city to accommodate the expected demand.

    In fact, the airline has confirmed that it will operate more than 120 flights per day during the peak of CES 2027, connecting Las Vegas with major business markets in the US and overseas. Its prepares include additional domestic frequencies and new nonstop international services from Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) and Taipei International Airport (TPE), two major Asian technology markets. Both routes will be operated by A350 widebody aircraft.

The airline has also scheduled individual flights to Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) and Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), which may be related to aircraft positioning for its CES operations.

    Delta is one of the largest operators of the A350-900.     Sources indicate that russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    In a recent development, trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he released a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    Recent findings suggest that “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Latest York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    According to recent reports, other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    It has been revealed that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of challenges, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    In a recent development, nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He mentioned it was “notable” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers noted they doubted very much would come from it.

    In a recent development, “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    It has been revealed that “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

    While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

    Industry observers note that well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has revealed aims to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

    As is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

    Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

    Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:.

    “Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

    Recent findings suggest that we’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary upcoming first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

    Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:.

    Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

    When it comes to the temporary newly introduced first class lounge, here are the details:.

    As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉.

    But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

    Two things stand out to me here:.

    It has been revealed that emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s fresh lounge aesthetic.

    We’ve just seen the opening of a upcoming temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

    The latest design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

    FAA Technician Only Unlocked The Door: Inside The Oversight Gap Behind The Nationwide Ground Stop

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours.
    • The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.
    • Sources indicate that so, what’s actually going on here?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We quickly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

    The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

    Sources indicate that so, what’s actually going on here? A fresh report sheds some more light on this….

    CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

    According to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

    That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

    FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”.

    Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

    This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”.

    With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

    Sources indicate that while the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

    A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”.

    DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl.

    It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

    That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

    Industry observers note that we have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to latest levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

    It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”.

    We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

    According to recent reports, while the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a new system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

    What do you make of this FAA contractor oversight situation?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, avelo Airlines' network for the winter 2026/27 season looks rather different to how it did in 2025/26.
    • Recent findings suggest that on the international side, scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, indicates that all of the cuts impact short-haul services to key leisure markets in Mexico and the Caribbean.
    • In a recent development, wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina is a common factor when examining Avelo's winter network versus 12 months ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, avelo Airlines' network for the winter 2026/27 season looks rather different to how it did in 2025/26. Most notably, 31 of the routes the carrier served this time last year are not being operated this time around, with 25 domestic and six international. Of the domestic cuts, a third are concentrated at one airport, highlighting the brutally competitive nature of the airline industry in the States.

    Recent findings suggest that on the international side, scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, indicates that all of the cuts impact short-haul services to key leisure markets in Mexico and the Caribbean. While the last year has seen Avelo make various route cuts, the airline is in flux, and it has a lot to look forward to fleet-wise with the Embraer E2 set to modernize its ops. The airline has ordered 50, with deliveries from 2028.

    In a recent development, wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina is a common factor when examining Avelo's winter network versus 12 months ago. Overall, the facility has lost winter service to nine destinations, four of which are in Florida: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW), Orlando International Airport (MCO), and West Palm Beach.

    Avelo Airlines' Current Operating Bases.

    The remaining five route cuts concerned services from Wilmington to destinations in the northeast of the US. These included major hubs such as Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), as well as smaller destinations such as Islip, Manchester, and Rochester.

    Avelo commented on its presence in Wilmington in a statement obtained earlier this year by Wilmington Biz.

    "Wilmington is also not a protected airport. Most of the affected routes cannot handle more than one airline serving them due to demand.".

    In a recent development, while Wilmington has been the hardest-hit airport by Avelo's winter cuts, it is far from the only US facility to have lost routes. Elsewhere in North Carolina, the carrier is no longer serving five destinations from Raleigh-Durham International (RDU) that it did this time last year: these are Albany, Fort Myers, Grand Rapids, Manchester, and Rochester. Of course, the cuts extend beyond North Carolina.

    It has been revealed that for instance, Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN) has lost three winter Avelo Airlines routes: William P. Hobby Airport (HOU), Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD). Wilmington in Delaware (ILG) saw three cuts, namely to Jacksonville (JAX), Nashville (BNA), and Raleigh-Durham, while Nashville itself lost Rochester.

    Returning to the state of North Carolina, Concord-Padgett Regional Airport (USA) no longer handles winter Avelo Airlines flights to West Palm Beach. Elsewhere, the American ultra-low-cost carrier also no longer flies from Islip to Lakeland Linder International Airport (LAL) in Florida in the winter. Still, it remains relatively busy, with 1,616 flights scheduled to operate this November. These will offer 300,784 seats.

    On the international side, Wilmington International Airport has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic. The carrier has also ceased its winter services to this popular Caribbean leisure destination from Bradley International Airport (BDL) in Windsor Locks, Connecticut, and Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU).

    In a recent development, windsor Locks has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Cancún International Airport (CUN) in Mexico, and the carrier has ceased winter service from both Windsor Locks and Raleigh-Durham to Sangster International Airport (MBJ) in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The cessation of these routes marked the end of Avelo Airlines' international flights, which had only commenced operations back in 2024.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

    Along those lines, there’s a major upgrade, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

    The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

    Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, fresh rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

    In a recent development, let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

    With that out of the way, let’s go over the details….

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

    It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a upcoming rewards structure. The card now offers:.

    According to recent reports, what has changed here is the newly introduced 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few fresh benefits that it didn’t previously offer:.

    The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

    Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the fresh 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

    As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a latest Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

    Industry observers note that applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

    As of now, it sounds like there are no plans to transition people to the newly introduced system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

    According to recent reports, the Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

    In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

    In a recent development, admittedly it’s hard to do an apples-to-apples comparison between personal and business cards, because at least in theory, they’re supposed to serve different purposes. So here’s my take:.

    So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

    Industry observers note that the Atmos Rewards Business Card has just undergone some major changes, though they don’t impact existing card members. For new applicants, the card now has a $195 annual fee, compared to the old fee of $70 for the manufacturer, and $25 per person.

    Recent findings suggest that the card is also getting a new set of benefits, including a new rewards structure, additional perks, and new incentives for spending. People will have varying takes as to whether these changes are positive or negative, depending on their consumer patterns.

    My biggest takeaway is that the bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending is excellent, and a great incentive to apply for the card.

    #65520. Latest Update: The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With Newly introduced 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1709 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With Newly introduced 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them.
    • Recent findings suggest that so who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the newly introduced 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one?
    • The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them. The 777-9 is meant to be the jet that carries the world's biggest long-haul airlines through the 2030s, but the program is about seven years behind its original 2020 service date, and the biggest customer has already turned away its first batch. For an industry that looks fleets decades ahead, that is a very awkward way to start a latest era.

    Recent findings suggest that so who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the newly introduced 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one? The answers involve Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansa, plus a rival Airbus that has already started delivering.

    The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore. According to an order book compiled by Airways Magazine at the end of May 2026, the 777X program stood at 619 orders: 521 777-9s, 63 777-8 freighters, and 35 passenger 777-8s, all of them for Emirates. That is a remarkable number for an aircraft that has not carried a single paying passenger, and it makes the 777X Boeing's most key widebody bet of the decade. Airways also noted that the problem is certification, not demand, which is a rare thing to say about a program this delayed.

    Emirates dominates the list. As reported by Emirates itself, its November 2025 Dubai Airshow deal added 65 more 777-9s, worth $38 billion at list prices, and lifted its total to 270 777Xs. The airline also holds options to convert part of that order into the 777-8 or the proposed, larger 777-10. Airways lists the split as 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, so the exact mix is still fluid. Qatar Airways is second with 124 aircraft, made up of 90 777-9s and 34 777-8 freighters, followed by Cathay Pacific with 35 and Singapore Airlines with 31.

    It has been revealed that british Airways and its parent IAG have 24, Lufthansa Group has 27 (20 passenger jets and seven freighters), Korean Air has 20, and ANA has 20, including two freighters. Air India, Etihad, and Ethiopian Airlines hold 10, 10, and 8. But a long list of customers only tells us who wants the jet. It indicates nothing about what each of them looks to retire in exchange, or how long they will have to keep the old aircraft flying while they wait.

    In a recent development, for most buyers, the answer is the Boeing 777-300ER, the best-selling long-haul widebody of its generation. Emirates alone flies 119 of them, plus 10 777-200LRs, according to its own fleet table. As noted by Simple Flying, the 777X is also pitched as a successor to high-capacity four-engine jets such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A380, which burn far more fuel and cost more to maintain.

    According to recent reports, the new jet's biggest selling point is efficiency. According to Simple Flying's analysis of range and capacity, the 777-9 seats around 426 passengers against roughly 396 on a 777-300ER, while keeping a nearly identical range. The GE9X engines are expected to deliver up to 10% better fuel efficiency than the GE90-115B engines on the older jet.

    The wing is the other trick: it spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters) in flight, but its tips fold to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.9 meters) on the ground so it still fits standard gates. Boeing's pitch to airlines is simple: keep the long range, burn less fuel, and spend less on maintenance than the aging jets on the ramp.

    Boeing 777-300ER vs. 777-9: the swap in numbers.

    7,370 nautical miles (13,649 km).

    7,285 nautical miles (13,492 km).

    242 feet, 4 inches (73.9 meters).

    251 feet, 9 inches (76.7 meters).

    GE9X (up to 10% better efficiency).

    On paper, that is a clean trade: more seats, similar range, lower fuel burn. The uncomfortable detail is that the older jets have to keep flying while the replacement is late, and that raises a very practical question about timing. Airways Magazine points out that carriers waiting on the 777-9 have had to stretch the lives of older 777-300ERs, A380s, and 747-400s, which adds maintenance, fuel, and cabin-product pressure with every extra year.

    In a recent development, lufthansa will be the first, with Boeing targeting a 2027 delivery. Emirates said in November 2025 that it expects its first 777-9 from the second quarter of 2027, and its Boeing deliveries stretch all the way to 2038. That means the airline will be swapping 777-300ERs for 777-9s for more than a decade, which is exactly why this story belongs to the 2030s rather than to next year. Emirates still flies 116 Airbus A380s as well, so the transition will be gradual rather than a clean break.

    Others will wait longer. According to Simple Flying, citing the Mainly Miles blog, Singapore Airlines' fleet plan demonstrates no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Lufthansa ahead in the queue. That timing matters because Singapore Airlines is also planning a newly introduced premium economy product around the aircraft, making the 777-9 part of a future cabin strategy as well as a fleet replacement program.

    In a recent development, even the schedule itself is soft. Airways Magazine reported that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford signaled the 777X would follow the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 into 2027 for certification. So queue position is one thing, but the airlines cannot simply take delivery because they are next in line. The more awkward problem is already sitting on Boeing's property: aircraft built years ago for customers that may no longer want them.

    Between 2019 and 2021, Boeing built around 30 777-9s before the program stalled, including aircraft earmarked for Emirates and Lufthansa, according to German aviation outlet aero.de. By the time they could be delivered, they would be about eight years old and technically behind the final production standard. That creates an unusual problem for a brand-fresh aircraft: the earliest examples are already old enough to require substantial work before an airline wants them.

    As reported by Simple Flying, Emirates rejected the first batch built for it because bringing those airframes up to the required standard would take extensive and costly rework. Boeing reportedly dismantled one early Emirates-bound 777-9 after the cost to fix it exceeded its value. Lufthansa has since mentioned, on its second-quarter earnings call, that it will refuse some of its earliest aircraft, with Boeing contributing financially to upgrade the rest.

    Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways has reportedly signaled that it does not want early-build aircraft either, so Boeing may pool the rejected jets and sell them in bundles. According to aero.de, an unnamed US airline is reportedly interested in 20 early 777-9s, which is striking because no major US carrier has ordered the type at all. A discounted early-build 777-9 could therefore find a new home, but the fact that airlines that ordered the aircraft in the first place are turning some away reveals just how unusual this delay has become.

    According to Simple Flying, Qatar Airways put the A350-1000 into service in February 2018, the 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and still was not certified at Farnborough 2026, and Airbus has already delivered 114 A350-1000s against 367 firm orders. Boeing, meanwhile, has delivered none of its more than 520 777-9s.

    It has been revealed that air Canada is the clearest example. As reported by Business Traveller, the airline ordered eight A350-1000s, with options on eight more, for delivery from the second half of 2030, to modernize a long-haul fleet that includes 19 777-300ERs. Business Traveller calls the A350-1000 a logical replacement for the 777-300ER, and indicates it brings a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) versus 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on the 777 family. No North American airline has ordered the 777-9, so for passengers in the US and Canada, the A350-1000 may arrive first.

    In a recent development, still, a head start is not the same as a better fit. The 777-9 carries more passengers, and for airlines that fill every seat, that may be the decisive metric. The A350-1000 offers the established nine-abreast cabin and a substantial operating track record, while Boeing's aircraft offers greater capacity and is aimed squarely at airlines that need to move huge numbers of passengers through constrained hubs. That leaves the 777-9 with a clear market, but a narrower one than the raw order total might suggest.

    Recent findings suggest that the honest answer is volume and density. Emirates and Qatar Airways run some of the busiest trunk routes in the world, and for those carriers, the 777-9's size is a feature rather than a flaw. An A350-1000 cannot match its seat count, and the A380 is out of production, so the 777-9 is effectively the last big twin-engine option left for airlines that need capacity above all else. That is the strongest argument Boeing has, and it is also why the aircraft is best suited to a relatively small group of mega-hub operators.

    The test comes in the next 18 months. If Lufthansa takes its first jet in 2027 and Emirates follows soon after, the long order book will start to look like a steady delivery stream. If certification slips again, as Airways Magazine warns could compress the entire handover and training timeline, more carriers may do what Air Canada did and look at the A350-1000 instead. The early-build jets will be worth watching too: how many Boeing can remarket, and at what price, will reveal just how costly the delay has been.

    Emirates has even signed options to stretch part of its order into the 777-10, a bigger variant Boeing is still studying. That may ultimately be the most revealing sign of all: the airlines that have waited longest for the 777-9 are still thinking about what comes after it. By 2035, the question may no longer be whether the 777-9 replaced the 777-300ER. It may be whether Boeing's biggest twinjet has finally found the narrow but extremely valuable market it was designed for.

    Breaking: Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female.
    • Industry observers note that today is (apparently) International Men’s Day.
    • According to recent reports, the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

    Industry observers note that today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

    According to recent reports, the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this important? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the company hopes to see that number grow in the future.

    I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

    I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”.

    It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and indicates “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

    Industry observers note that what’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

    Industry observers note that in fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

    Recent findings suggest that while we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

    What do you make of Finnair’s all-male flight?

    The House has a new lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.
    • Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.

    Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    Sources indicate that the House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    Industry observers note that "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    It has been revealed that of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-indicates; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, mentioned. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    Recent findings suggest that “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    Sources indicate that “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., mentioned. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
    • Industry observers note that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
    • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    Industry observers note that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    It has been revealed that now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it states this:.

    Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Sources indicate that then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    According to recent reports, as of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.
